chapter.name: Proportional Reasoning-2
chapter.blurb: Recap of testing two-term ratios for proportionality by cross multiplication; reading a map's Representative Fraction as a ratio and converting between map distance and actual distance; ratios with more than two terms and scaling every term by the same factor; dividing a whole quantity into parts in a given ratio, including decimal-term ratios and triangle angle-sum/side-ratio reasoning; converting ratios and percentages into pie-chart sector angles and reading pie charts; and direct proportion (the rule of three) versus inverse proportion (xy = k), including combined work-rate problems.

scope_in.item: Represent a relationship between two quantities using ratio notation a : b, recapping that a proportional relationship is one where the quantities change by the same factor
Test whether two given two-term ratios a : b and c : d are proportional using cross multiplication (a x d = b x c), and write the result using the a : b :: c : d notation
Interpret a map's Representative Fraction (RF), given as a ratio such as 1 : 60,00,000, as map distance : actual (ground) distance
Convert a given map distance to the actual geographical distance, or an actual distance to a map distance, using the RF, including converting cm to km
Write and interpret a ratio with three or more terms (a : b : c : d) to compare more than two quantities that all change by the same factor
Given a multi-term ratio and the actual quantity corresponding to one term, find the actual quantities of the other terms by scaling every term by the same factor
Divide a total quantity into two or more parts in a given ratio, including ratios with decimal terms, using the formula (whole x term) / (sum of terms) for each part
Apply the ratio-division method to word problems such as sharing time, books, coins or profit in a given ratio, including finding the value of a ratio-divided quantity
Use the angle-sum property of a triangle (180 degrees) together with a given ratio of angles to find each angle of the triangle
Reason, using the triangle inequality, about whether a triangle can be constructed from a given ratio of side lengths, and whether all triangles with that side ratio must be congruent to each other
Convert a set of category frequencies, or a ratio, into pie-chart sector angles using (frequency / total) x 360 degrees, simplifying the underlying ratio by its HCF first where helpful
Convert a set of percentages into pie-chart sector angles using (percentage / 100) x 360 degrees
Read a given pie chart (with sector angles, fractions or percentages) to find quantities, compare categories, and identify the most or least common category
State and use the rule of three for a direct proportion: given a : b :: c : d, find the unknown fourth term as d = (b x c) / a

Distinguish direct proportion (both quantities change by the same factor in the same direction) from inverse proportion (one quantity changes by a factor n while the other changes by the factor 1/n), using tables of corresponding values

State and apply the inverse-proportion relation x1 x y1 = x2 x y2 to solve word problems: workers and days, pumps/taps and time to fill a tank, machines and days, and food provisions and number of people
Solve combined work-rate problems where two agents work together on the same task, by adding their unit-time work rates and taking the reciprocal of the combined rate to find the time taken together

scope_out.item: Measuring actual distances on a printed map with a ruler, or making an accurate scale drawing/sketch of a room
scope_out.reason: These are hands-on classroom activities (the map-reading 'Try it' and the Map Making Activity note to the teacher on pp. 56-57) that need a physical map or room to measure; no map image or physical measurement is available to build a written question around, so only the numeric RF-conversion skill is tested

scope_out.item: Physically constructing a triangle or a pie chart with a compass, ruler and protractor as a step-by-step drawing procedure
scope_out.reason: The construction steps shown (pie-chart steps 1-7 on pp. 61-62, triangle constructions on p. 60) are drawing instructions that cannot be assessed in a written answer; only the underlying angle/ratio arithmetic and the reasoning about whether a construction is possible are testable

scope_out.item: Compound ratios formed by combining two separate ratios that share a common term (e.g. combining a : b and b : c into a : b : c)
scope_out.reason: This technique is never shown in the chapter; every multi-term ratio here is given directly, not built by combining two shorter ratios

scope_out.item: Simple interest, compound interest, profit and loss, or percentage increase/decrease as a topic
scope_out.reason: Percentages appear only once, converting given percentages directly into pie-chart angles (p. 62); no interest, profit/loss or percentage-change formula is taught

scope_out.item: Speed-distance-time as a formula-based topic in its own right
scope_out.reason: Speed and time appear only as one worked example of an inverse-proportion pair (motorcycle/car travel time, pp. 63-64) and in Figure-it-out word problems solved with the inverse-proportion product rule, never via a taught distance = speed x time formula

scope_out.item: Graphs of direct or inverse proportion, or algebraic function notation such as y = kx or y = k/x
scope_out.reason: The chapter states the relations in words and with x1y1 = x2y2; no plotted graph of a proportional relationship or function notation is used

scope_out.item: Similar figures or geometric scale factor of shapes (enlargement/reduction of a figure)
scope_out.reason: Not covered in this chapter; every ratio here compares numeric quantities (workers, spices, distances, angles), not the geometric similarity of two shapes

scope_out.item: Combined work-rate problems with three or more agents, staggered start times, or partially completed work left for another agent
scope_out.reason: Every combined-work example and Figure-it-out question in the chapter pairs exactly two agents (or a small fixed number of identical pumps) working the whole time together; staggered starts or partial work are never used

concepts.name: Testing whether two ratios are proportional
concepts.description: Checking two two-term ratios a : b and c : d for proportionality using cross multiplication a x d = b x c, and interpreting the result in real contexts such as recipes.
concepts.idea: Two ratios are proportional if one can be scaled to the other by a single common factor; cross multiplication gives a fast test for this without having to find the factor.
concepts.rule: For ratios a : b and c : d, they are proportional (written a : b :: c : d) exactly when a x d = b x c.
concepts.example: For 6 : 3 and 4 : 2, the cross products are 6 x 2 = 12 and 3 x 4 = 12. Since these are equal, the ratios are proportional.

concepts.name: Ratios in maps (Representative Fraction)
concepts.description: Interpreting a map's Representative Fraction (RF) as map distance : actual distance, and converting between map distance and real geographical distance using this ratio, including unit conversion from cm to km.
concepts.idea: A map scale ratio like 1 : 60,00,000 is applied like any ratio to convert a measured map distance into the real distance it represents, or the reverse.
concepts.rule: If RF = 1 : k, then actual distance = (map distance) x k, in the same length unit as measured, then converted to the required unit; conversely, map distance = (actual distance, in the same unit) / k.
concepts.example: 1 : 60,00,000 means 1 cm on the map represents 60,00,000 cm = 60 km on the ground, so 2 cm on the map represents 120 km.

concepts.name: Ratios with more than two terms
concepts.description: Writing and scaling ratios with three or more terms (a : b : c : d) when one term's real quantity is known, keeping every term scaled by the same factor.
concepts.idea: A multi-term ratio behaves like a two-term ratio extended to more quantities: every term must be scaled by the same factor to preserve the proportional relationship.
concepts.rule: If a : b : c : d is a ratio and the actual quantity for one term is known, find the common scale factor from that term (new value divided by its ratio term), then multiply every other term by that same factor.
concepts.example: The spice ratio coriander : chilli : toor dal : fenugreek = 8 : 4 : 2 : 1. With only 2 chillies (half of 4), every term is scaled by 0.5, giving 4 : 2 : 1 : 0.5.

concepts.name: Dividing a whole in a given ratio (two or more terms)
concepts.description: Splitting a total quantity x into parts according to a ratio with two or more terms (possibly with decimal terms), using the formula x x (term) / (sum of terms) for each part, and applying this to word problems including triangle angle-sum and side-ratio reasoning.
concepts.idea: Dividing a whole by a ratio means treating the terms of the ratio as the number of equal shares each part gets out of the total number of shares.
concepts.rule: To divide a quantity x in the ratio a : b : c : ..., each part = x x (that term) / (a + b + c + ...).
concepts.example: Dividing 110 units of concrete in the ratio 1 : 1.5 : 3 (sum 5.5) gives 110 x 1 / 5.5 = 20, 110 x 1.5 / 5.5 = 30, and 110 x 3 / 5.5 = 60.

concepts.name: Constructing and reading pie charts from ratios
concepts.description: Converting a frequency/ratio distribution, or given percentages, into pie-chart sector angles using part/total x 360 degrees, simplifying the ratio first where helpful, and reading a given pie chart to answer questions about the data.
concepts.idea: A pie chart divides the full 360 degrees of a circle in the same proportion as the data's ratio, so each category's angle is found the same way a whole is divided in a given ratio, using 360 degrees as the whole.
concepts.rule: For a category with frequency f out of total S (or ratio term t out of ratio-sum T), the sector angle = (f / S) x 360 degrees (or (t / T) x 360 degrees). Given percentages, angle = (percentage / 100) x 360 degrees.
concepts.example: Grades A : B : C : D : E = 12 : 10 : 8 : 6 : 4, simplest form 6 : 5 : 4 : 3 : 2 (sum 20). Grade A angle = (6 / 20) x 360 degrees = 108 degrees.

concepts.name: Direct and inverse proportion, including combined work rates
concepts.description: Using the rule of three to find an unknown fourth term of a direct proportion a : b :: c : d (d = bc/a); recognising and solving inverse-proportion problems where xy = k stays constant; solving combined work/rate problems using unit work rates.
concepts.idea: Two quantities are directly proportional when they change by the same factor in the same direction; they are inversely proportional when one changes by a factor n while the other changes by the factor 1/n, so their product stays constant.
concepts.rule: Direct: a : b :: c : d gives d = (b x c) / a. Inverse: if x1, y1 and x2, y2 are corresponding inversely-proportional values, x1 x y1 = x2 x y2. Combined work: the rate of working together is the sum of the individual unit-time work rates, and the time taken is 1 divided by the combined rate.
concepts.example: 20 workers take 4 days for a job; with 10 workers (half as many), the days double: 10 x y2 = 20 x 4, so y2 = 8 days.
